title: The Revelation of Jesus Christ
subtitle: Revelation 1:1–8
description: The revelation's chain of delivery, the blessing on those who hear and obey, grace and peace to the seven churches, and the coming one every eye will see.
paragraphs: The last book of the Bible opens by tracing its own chain of custody. It is “the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass,” and “He made it known by sending His angel to His servant John,” “who testifies to everything he saw.” What John saw is named twice over in one breath: “This is the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ.”

Over the reading of it hangs a blessing, the book's first of seven. “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy,” the opening says, “and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near.”

Then the book turns to its readers as a letter. “Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was and is to come,” John writes to the seven churches in the province of Asia, “and from the seven spirits before His throne,” “and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.”

The greeting rises into praise. “To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood,” John writes, the one “who has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,” and he assigns him the glory and power forever and ever, and seals it with Amen.

Last comes a sight pointed past the page. “Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him,” “even those who pierced Him,” and the tribes of the earth will mourn because of him. Above the whole opening stands the speaker's name for himself. “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and was and is to come,” the Almighty.

title: On the Island of Patmos
subtitle: Revelation 1:9–20
description: John, brother and partner in tribulation, exiled on Patmos, turns toward the voice and sees one like a son of man among the lampstands, holding the seven stars.
paragraphs: The writer introduces himself the way he wants to be known: not above the churches but inside their trouble with them. “I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus, was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus.” Patmos was an island exile, and the book states his offense in one line: the word of God, and his testimony about Jesus.

“On the Lord’s day I was in the Spirit, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet,” saying, “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches”: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea, seven real congregations in the province of Asia, named in the order a messenger would reach them.

John turned toward the voice. “And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man, dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest.” The description builds piece by piece. “The hair of His head was white like wool, as white as snow, and His eyes were like a blazing fire. His feet were like polished bronze refined in a furnace, and His voice was like the roar of many waters. He held in His right hand seven stars, and a sharp double-edged sword came from His mouth. His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.”

The seer's response is the one the sight produces. “When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man.” But the figure placed his right hand on him and spoke: “Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, the Living One.” His claim is resurrection stated flatly: “I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever!” and “I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.”

Then the commission is repeated with its scope: “Therefore write down the things you have seen, the things that are, and the things that will happen after this.” And the first symbol is interpreted by the speaker himself, the book's own pattern for its imagery: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.” The risen Christ walks among his churches, and the letters that follow are dictated from inside that picture.

title: Ephesus and Smyrna
subtitle: Revelation 2:1–11
description: Ephesus, orthodox and persevering, has left its first love; Smyrna, poor and slandered, receives no rebuke and the promise that the second death will not hurt it.
paragraphs: The vision turns into dictation: seven letters, each opening with a portrait of the speaker drawn from what John saw among the lampstands, and each ending with the same summons, “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

Ephesus hears from the one “who holds the seven stars in His right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands.” The praise is real and specific: “I know your deeds, your labor, and your perseverance,” and “you have tested and exposed as liars those who falsely claim to be apostles.” “Without growing weary, you have persevered and endured many things for the sake of My name.” This is a church that guards the truth and does not quit.

Then the sentence the letter is remembered by: “But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love.” The remedy is memory and return: “Repent and perform the deeds you did at first.” The warning under it is the lampstand itself. If they do not repent, “I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place.” One credit is added even inside the rebuke: “You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.” And the promise to the one who overcomes reaches back to Eden: “I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God.”

Smyrna's letter is shorter, and it contains no rebuke at all. The speaker names himself “the First and the Last, who died and returned to life,” the exact credential a suffering church needs. “I know your affliction and your poverty,” he says, and then the parenthesis that reverses the ledger: “though you are rich!” He knows “the slander of those who falsely claim to be Jews, but are in fact a synagogue of Satan,” opponents in that city whose claim the speaker refuses. What is coming is named before it comes: “you will suffer tribulation for ten days.” And over the suffering stands the letter's charge and crown: “Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” Its promise closes the pair: “The one who overcomes will not be harmed by the second death.”

title: Pergamum and Thyatira
subtitle: Revelation 2:12–29
description: Pergamum holds fast where Satan's throne is yet tolerates Balaam's compromise; Thyatira's works grow while it tolerates the woman the letter calls Jezebel.
paragraphs: Pergamum hears from “the One who holds the sharp, double-edged sword,” and the letter starts with the hardest address in the seven: “I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits, yet you hold fast to My name.” In that city, loyalty had a name and a grave: “My faithful witness Antipas, who was killed among you where Satan dwells,” and still, the letter says, they did not deny their faith in him.

The charge is compromise, not cowardice: “some of you hold to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites” so they would “eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality,” the old Moabite snare from the wilderness years running again in a Roman city, and alongside it the teaching of the Nicolaitans. The command is single: “Therefore repent!” The alternative is the sword of the opening portrait turned inward: “I will come to you shortly and wage war against them with the sword of My mouth.” To the one who overcomes, the promises are intimate and strange: “I will give the hidden manna,” and he will “give him a white stone inscribed with a new name, known only to the one who receives it.”

Thyatira's letter is the longest, from the Son of God “whose eyes are like a blazing fire and whose feet are like polished bronze.” The praise runs ahead of the rebuke: “your love, your faith, your service, your perseverance,” and, rare among the seven, growth: “your latest deeds are greater than your first.”

The rebuke targets tolerance. “You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess. By her teaching she misleads My servants to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols.” The letter uses Ahab's queen's name for a present teacher, and the patience shown her is stated before the judgment: though he had “given her time to repent of her immorality, she is unwilling.” What follows is severe: “I will cast her onto a bed of sickness,” and “I will strike her children dead,” so that “all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts, and I will repay each of you according to your deeds.”

To the rest, who have not learned the so-called deep things of Satan, the burden is deliberately light: “I will place no further burden upon you” than to “hold fast to what you have until I come.” The overcoming promise is the largest yet: authority over the nations, for “He will rule them with an iron scepter and shatter them like pottery,” and, last and quietest, “And I will give him the morning star.”

title: Sardis and Philadelphia
subtitle: Revelation 3:1–13
description: Sardis has a name for being alive and is dead, with a faithful few in white; Philadelphia, of little strength, receives an open door no one can shut.
paragraphs: Sardis hears from the one who holds the seven spirits of God and the seven stars, and the letter opens with a reputation corrected by an autopsy: “you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead.” The command is a single waking: “Wake up and strengthen what remains, which is about to die,” for, the speaker says, “I have found your deeds incomplete in the sight of My God.” The memory is the treatment: remember what you received and heard, keep it, and repent. The alternative is a visit no one schedules: “I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour when I will come upon you.”

Yet even here there are exceptions, named with care: “you do have a few people in Sardis who have not soiled their garments,” and “they will walk with Me in white,” because they are worthy. The overcoming promise for this near-dead church is the Book of Life itself: “I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life, but I will confess his name before My Father and His angels.”

Philadelphia's letter contains no rebuke at all. Its speaker is “the One who is holy and true, who holds the key of David. What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open.” The door is the letter's first gift: “Behold, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut.” The church's strength is described with unusual tenderness: “you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name.”

Its opponents, the same synagogue of Satan named at Smyrna, will be reversed into witnesses: “I will make them come and bow down at your feet, and they will know that I love you.” Then the promise bound to their perseverance: “Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth.” How that keeping works is a question readers have answered differently for centuries; the letter itself states the promise and its ground, and moves on. The present charge is short: “I am coming soon. Hold fast to what you have, so that no one will take your crown.” And the overcomer is made architecture in God's house, a pillar who will “never again leave it,” inscribed with three names: “the name of My God, and the name of the city of My God,” the new Jerusalem, “and My new name.”

title: Laodicea
subtitle: Revelation 3:14–22
description: Laodicea, lukewarm and self-deceived about its wealth, is counseled to buy true gold, white garments, and eye salve, and hears the knock at its own door.
paragraphs: The last letter has the strangest opening title of the seven: its speaker is “the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God’s creation.” Against that witness, the church's own self-testimony will not survive the letter.

There is no praise in this one, and the charge is a temperature. “I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot. How I wish you were one or the other!” Then the famous sentence, split in the text by its own explanation: “So because you are lukewarm,” “neither hot nor cold,” “I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!”

The root of the lukewarmness is a false ledger. The church's own words are quoted back at it, and they stand as their own sentence: “I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.” The speaker's audit reads the opposite column: “you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked.”

Yet the letter to the worst church carries some of the book's warmest counsel. “I counsel you to buy from Me gold refined by fire so that you may become rich,” “white garments so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed,” “and salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see.” Every item answers the audit point for point: true wealth for poverty, clothing for nakedness, sight for blindness, all of it bought from the speaker himself. And the rebuke is reframed as love's habit: “Those I love I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent.”

Then comes the picture the letter is loved for: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.” The Christ who walks among the lampstands stands at this church's door as a guest, waiting to be let in by anyone who hears. And the promise to its overcomer is the highest seat in the seven letters: “To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne, just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne.” From the door, for those who open it, to the throne.

title: A Door Open in Heaven
subtitle: Revelation 4:1–11
description: A door stands open in heaven: the throne, the emerald rainbow, the twenty-four elders, and the four living creatures crying holy, holy, holy without ceasing.
paragraphs: The letters dictated, the vision opens upward. “After this I looked and saw a door standing open in heaven,” John writes, and the trumpet voice from Patmos speaks again: “Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things.” His report of the ascent is one line: “At once I was in the Spirit, and I saw a throne standing in heaven, with someone seated on it.”

Everything in the room arranges itself around that throne. “The One seated there looked like jasper and carnelian,” John says, describing by precious stone and color rather than by form, “and a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne.” Around it “sat twenty-four elders dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads,” on thrones of their own. “From the throne came flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder. Before the throne burned seven torches of fire. These are the seven spirits of God,” the book glosses, explaining its own symbol as it goes. And “before the throne was something like a sea of glass, as clear as crystal.”

At the center, closest to the throne, are the four living creatures, covered with eyes in front and back: “The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face like a man, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight.” Each has six wings and is covered with eyes all around and within, and their worship never pauses: “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”

Whenever the creatures give glory, the elders answer with their crowns. They fall down before the one who lives forever and ever and cast their crowns before the throne, and their song gives the reason the whole book will keep returning to: “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things; by Your will they exist and were created.” Before any seal is opened or any judgment falls, the book shows its readers who sits at the center, and what he is owed.

title: The Scroll and the Lamb
subtitle: Revelation 5:1–14
description: No one is found worthy to open the sealed scroll, until the Lion announced is seen as a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, and heaven sings the new song.
paragraphs: In the right hand of the one on the throne sits the book's central object: “a scroll in the right hand of the One seated on the throne. It had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals.” A mighty angel puts the question to all creation: “Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?” The answer is a silence wide enough to hold heaven, earth, and under the earth: “no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it.”

The seer's response is grief, not curiosity. John “began to weep bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or look inside it.” An elder stops the weeping with an announcement: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed” and can open the scroll and its seven seals.

Then John looks for the Lion, and what he sees is the book's great surprise, staged deliberately. “Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne,” encircled by the creatures and the elders. “The Lamb had seven horns and seven eyes, which represent the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.” Announced as a Lion, seen as a slain Lamb standing: the book does not explain the pairing, it simply sets the two side by side and lets the worship explain it.

The Lamb takes the scroll, and the throne room breaks open in song. The creatures and elders fall down holding harps and “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints,” and the new song is addressed to the Lamb: “Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. You have made them to be a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth.”

Around that song a wider one gathers, angels beyond counting, “myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,” crying, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!” And last, every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea answers: “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!” The creatures say Amen, the elders fall down, and the scroll is ready to open.

title: Four Horsemen
subtitle: Revelation 6:1–8
description: The Lamb opens the first four seals: the white horse, the red horse taking peace, the black horse with famine prices, and the pale green horse named Death.
paragraphs: The Lamb begins to open the seals, and each of the first four is announced the same way: John hears “one of the four living creatures say in a voice like thunder,” and the summons goes out, and a horse and rider appear.

First, the white horse: “I looked and saw a white horse, and its rider held a bow. And he was given a crown, and he rode out to overcome and conquer.” Conquest rides out crowned and bent on more conquest; the book gives the rider a bow and a purpose and no name, and readers have argued for centuries over who he is. The vision itself simply lets him ride.

Second, the red: “another horse went forth. It was bright red, and its rider was granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another. And he was given a great sword.” Peace here is not broken from outside; permission is granted for it to be taken, and the earth does the slaying itself.

Third, the black: “I looked and saw a black horse, and its rider held in his hand a pair of scales.” Scales mean rationing, and a voice from among the creatures sets the prices like a market announcement: “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine.” A denarius was a laborer's day wage. A day's work buys a day's bread for one, or three days of the cheaper grain, while the luxuries of oil and wine stand untouched: scarcity measured so that the working poor starve at full employment.

Fourth, the last horse is named by its color and its rider together: “I looked and saw a pale green horse. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed close behind.” Their commission is the summary of the other three: “they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth.” Sword, famine, plague, beasts: war, scarcity, pestilence, and the wild, gathered under one rider, and the grave walking behind him to receive the harvest.

title: How Long, O Lord
subtitle: Revelation 6:9–17
description: Under the altar the martyrs cry how long and receive white robes and a wait; the sixth seal shakes the sky until every rank of humanity hides in the caves.
paragraphs: The fifth seal opens not on a horse but on an altar, and under it, people: “when the Lamb opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld.” They are not silent. Their cry is the episode's title and one of the book's most human sounds: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You judge those who dwell upon the earth and avenge our blood?”

The answer is a robe and a wait: “each of them was given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer,” until the number is full: “until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed, just as they had been killed.” Vindication is promised and postponed in the same sentence, and the postponement itself has a measure: more witnesses are still to die. The book does not hide that cost from its readers; it puts the martyrs' question in the martyrs' own words and lets the answer stand.

The sixth seal breaks the sky: “there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red,” and “the stars of the sky fell to the earth like unripe figs dropping from a tree shaken by a great wind. The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place.”

Then the vision counts the hiding: kings of the earth, nobles, commanders, the rich, the mighty, every slave and free man, the whole social order at once, in caves and among rocks. Their prayer is the Bible's strangest, addressed to the rocks themselves: “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb. For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?” The question hangs unanswered over the chapter break: who indeed. The next vision exists to answer it.

title: Sealed and Uncountable
subtitle: Revelation 7:1–17
description: The winds are held until God's servants are sealed: 144,000 heard, tribe by tribe, and then a multitude no one could count, washed in the blood of the Lamb.
paragraphs: Between the sixth seal and the seventh, the vision pauses, and the pause is an answer. Four angels stand at the earth's four corners holding back its winds, and another angel rises from the east carrying the seal of the living God. His order is a stay of execution: “Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God.” Before anything else is harmed, God's own are marked.

Then John hears a number, exact and countable: “I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel,” twelve thousand from each tribe as the roll is called: Judah first, then Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin. The list is the book's own arrangement, with Levi counted among the tribes and Joseph and Manasseh both named, and readers have long disagreed about whether the number is arithmetic or symbol. The vision states the number, calls the roll, and moves on.

What John sees next cannot be counted at all. “After this I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands.” Their shout is the short creed of the book: “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” And every angel around the throne falls facedown with a sevenfold answer: “Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever!”

An elder tests the seer: who are these in white robes, and where have they come from? John hands the question back, and the elder's answer names their road: “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” Washed white in blood: the book lets the paradox stand without sanding it down. “For this reason, they are before the throne of God and serve Him day and night in His temple; and the One seated on the throne will spread His tabernacle over them.”

Their future is described in the words of older prophecy: “Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst; nor will the sun beat down upon them, nor any scorching heat.” And the reason gathers the whole book into one sentence, the Lamb at the center doing a shepherd's work: “For the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. ’He will lead them to springs of living water,’ and ’God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’”

title: Silence, Then Trumpets
subtitle: Revelation 8:1–13
description: The seventh seal opens into half an hour of silence; the saints' prayers rise on the golden altar; then the trumpets strike the earth, sea, waters, and sky in thirds.
paragraphs: The seventh seal opens, and heaven does the most startling thing in the book so far: nothing. “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the songs, the thunder, and the martyrs' shouting, the throne room holds its breath, and in the silence seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets.

Before any trumpet sounds, prayer takes the stage. An angel with a golden censer stands at the altar: “He was given much incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne. And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God from the hand of the angel.” Then the same censer is filled with fire from the altar and reversed: “the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and hurled it to the earth,” and thunder, lightning, and an earthquake answer. The prayers of the saints and the judgments of God travel in the same vessel.

The trumpets strike in thirds. At the first, “hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass.” At the second, “something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea turned to blood,” and “a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.”

At the third, “a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven and landed on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood,” and the waters turned bitter: “many people died from the bitter waters.” At the fourth, “a third of the sun and moon and stars were struck,” and a third of the day and the night lost their light. A third at a time: the judgments of the trumpets are measured, partial, and announced as such, terrible and deliberately not yet total.

Above the darkened earth flies a single eagle, crying in a loud voice the book's new refrain: “Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!” Three trumpets remain, and each now has a name: a woe.

title: The Locusts and the Army
subtitle: Revelation 9:1–21
description: From the opened pit, limited locusts torment for five months; the Euphrates angels release an army of two hundred million; and the rest did not repent.
paragraphs: The fifth trumpet opens the earth downward. John sees “a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, and it was given the key to the pit of the Abyss.” The pit opens, and “smoke rose out of it like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the pit.” Out of the smoke comes the plague: “out of the smoke, locusts descended on the earth, and they were given power like that of the scorpions of the earth.”

These locusts are given limits as precise as the trumpets' thirds. “They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree, but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads.” And their weapon is pain without death: “not given power to kill them, but only to torment them for five months,” and “their torment was like the stinging of a scorpion.” The seal of chapter 7 now shows its purpose, and the torment's cruelty is its boundary: “In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, but death will escape them.”

Their appearance is assembled from armies and animals at once: “the locusts looked like horses prepared for battle,” with crowns like gold and faces like men. “They had hair like that of women, and teeth like those of lions,” breastplates of iron, and “the sound of their wings was like the roar of many horses and chariots rushing into battle.” They have a king, and his name is given in two languages like a wanted notice: “They were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon.” Both names mean destroyer. Then the count of woes advances: “The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow.”

The sixth trumpet releases an army instead of a plague. A voice from the golden altar gives the order: “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” They had been kept for a scheduled hour: “the four angels who had been prepared for this hour and day and month and year were released to kill a third of mankind.” Their cavalry is counted the way the 144,000 were counted, by hearing: “the number of mounted troops was two hundred million; I heard their number.”

The horses kill from both ends. Their riders wear breastplates the colors of fire, sapphire, and sulfur, the horses' heads are like lions' heads, and “out of their mouths proceeded fire, smoke, and sulfur. A third of mankind was killed by the three plagues of fire, smoke, and sulfur that proceeded from their mouths.” Their tails are like snakes, with heads to harm.

Then the chapter lands its bleakest sentence, and it is not about the dead: “the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not repent of the works of their hands. They did not stop worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk.” And the inventory closes without a turn: “they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft.” The woes were never only punishments; in the book's telling they are also summonses, and the summons is refused.

title: The Small Scroll
subtitle: Revelation 10:1–11
description: A mighty angel holds a small scroll lying open; the seven thunders are sealed; the oath declares no more delay; and John eats the scroll, sweet and bitter.
paragraphs: Between the sixth and seventh trumpets the vision pauses again, as it paused between the sixth and seventh seals, and the pause has a person in it: “another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow above his head. His face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire.” In his hand lay “a small scroll, which lay open,” and his stance spans the world of the trumpets: “He placed his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land.”

His cry sounds like a lion's roar, and seven thunders answer with voices. John prepares to write, as he has written everything, and is stopped: “When the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to put it in writing.” A voice from heaven gives the book's only order to conceal: “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.” In a book that exists so that servants will know what must take place, one message stays sealed. The telling records the sealing and does not guess at the contents; there is nothing to guess from.

Then the angel swears. He lifts his hand to heaven and swears “by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and everything in it, the earth and everything in it, and the sea and everything in it,” and the oath's content is a deadline ending: “There will be no more delay!” The mystery will not trail off into endless postponement: “the mystery of God will be fulfilled, just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets.”

What remains for John himself is the small scroll, and the instruction is the strangest in the book: he is to eat it. “It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.” His report confirms both halves exactly: “it was as sweet as honey in my mouth,” and “when I had eaten it, my stomach turned bitter.” An older prophet, Ezekiel, once ate a scroll in the same way; here the eating commissions the seer for the woes still to come. The episode ends with the order that explains it: “You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings.”

title: The Two Witnesses
subtitle: Revelation 11:1–19
description: The temple is measured and the court trampled; two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed and celebrated over, rise, and ascend; the seventh trumpet announces the kingdom.
paragraphs: The interlude continues with a measuring line. John is handed a rod: “I was given a measuring rod like a staff” and told, “Go and measure the temple of God and the altar, and count the number of worshipers there.” But the measurement has a boundary, and the boundary is a surrender: “Do not measure it, because it has been given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for 42 months.” The inner sanctuary is measured and kept; the outer court is handed over. The book does not explain the distinction, and its readers have mapped it many ways; the vision simply draws the line where it draws it.

At the center of the trampling stand two figures: “I will empower my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.” The book interprets its own symbol and names no names: “These witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.” Their protection is absolute while their testimony lasts: “fire proceeds from their mouths and devours their enemies.” Their powers are the powers of the old stories, drought and plague: they “have power to shut the sky so that no rain will fall during the days of their prophecy,” and “power to turn the waters into blood” and strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish. Readers have seen Moses and Elijah in them for centuries; the book lets the resemblance stand and gives them no other identity than witness.

When the testimony is finished, protection ends by design: “the beast that comes up from the Abyss will wage war with them, and will overpower and kill them.” It is the beast's first appearance in the book, arriving here. “Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city,” the city the text names with two borrowed names, “figuratively called Sodom and Egypt,” and locates with one clause: “where their Lord was also crucified.” For three and a half days the world files past the corpses and forbids them burial, and “those who dwell on the earth will gloat over them and celebrate and send one another gifts, because these two prophets had tormented them.”

Then the reversal, timed to the half week: “after the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them.” A voice calls them home with two words, and “they went up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watched them.” In the same hour an earthquake levels “a tenth of the city collapsed” and kills seven thousand, “and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven,” the first repentance-shaped response in the trumpet chapters, wrung out of terror.

“The second woe has passed. Behold, the third woe is coming shortly.” Then the seventh trumpet finally sounds, and heaven answers with the loudest announcement in the book: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.” The elders fall on their faces with the interpretation: “You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign. The nations were enraged, and Your wrath has come,” the hour to judge the dead, reward the prophets and saints, “and to destroy those who destroy the earth.” And the vision's last sight is inside the opened temple of heaven, where “the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple,” with lightning, thunder, earthquake, and hail around it.

title: The Woman and the Dragon
subtitle: Revelation 12:1–17
description: A woman clothed with the sun, a huge red dragon, a child caught up to the throne, war in heaven, and the dragon's short time of pursuit on earth.
paragraphs: The book now stops the sequence of seals and trumpets and shows the war behind the war, in signs. “And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. She was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth.” Readers have named her Israel, and Mary, and the church across the centuries, and the sign itself argues for scale over single identity: she wears the sun. The telling follows the vision, which never pauses to settle the name.

The second sign is her enemy: “a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven royal crowns on his heads. His tail swept a third of the stars from the sky, hurling them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth.”

The birth happens in two swift strokes, and its whole earthly life is passed over in one of them: “she gave birth to a son, a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter. And her child was caught up to God and to His throne.” Between the birth and the catching up stand the cross and the empty tomb, but the sign is interested in the dragon's failure: the child he waited to devour is beyond his reach. “And the woman fled into the wilderness, where God had prepared a place for her to be nourished for 1,260 days,” the witnesses' number again, protection measured in the same units as persecution.

Then the war the sign conceals breaks into the open: “a war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back.” The result is an eviction: “the dragon was not strong enough, and no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels.” And the hurled dragon is named with every name he owns: “the great dragon was hurled down,” “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him.”

Heaven's voice interprets the eviction as victory: “Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of His Christ. For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down,” “he who accuses them day and night before our God.” The brothers' part in the conquest is stated as a recipe anyone can check against the martyrs under the altar: “They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony,” and “they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death.” But the voice's joy has an edge, because the eviction has a destination: “woe to the earth and the sea; with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time.”

The short time is spent in pursuit, and the woman escapes it: “the woman was given two wings of a great eagle” to fly to her place, where “she was nourished for a time, and times, and half a time,” the 1,260 days in the older prophet's arithmetic. The serpent pours a river from his mouth to sweep her away, and “the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth.” Blocked from the woman, “the dragon was enraged at the woman and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus.” The chapter ends there, with the dragon on the shore of the sea, and the war turning toward everyone else.

title: The Two Beasts
subtitle: Revelation 13:1–18
description: A beast from the sea with the dragon's leased authority for forty-two months; a lamb-like second beast speaking like a dragon; the mark, and the number of a man, 666.
paragraphs: From the shore where the dragon stands, the war takes institutional shape. “Then I saw a beast with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea,” wearing ten royal crowns and “blasphemous names on its heads.” It is a composite of the older vision's beasts in Daniel, leopard, bear, and lion in one body: “The beast I saw was like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority.”

Its credential is a resurrection imitation. “One of the heads of the beast appeared to have been mortally wounded. But the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast.” Worship follows the marvel, and the worship is doubled: they worshiped the dragon who authorized the beast, and the beast, with a hymn that parodies the song of Moses: “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?”

The authority is real and it is leased, with a term: the beast speaks arrogant and blasphemous words, given “authority to act for 42 months,” the holy city's trampling time. It opens its mouth “to slander His name and His tabernacle,” those who dwell in heaven. And the lease includes the saints: “the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them,” with authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation, and worship from everyone “whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain.” Over that bleak paragraph the book sets its own instruction to the church inside it: “Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints.”

The second beast works the first beast's publicity. John sees “another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon.” It performs great signs on the first beast's behalf, “even causing fire from heaven to come down to earth in the presence of the people,” and by the signs it deceives the earth's dwellers into making “an image to the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived.” Then propaganda becomes enforcement: the second beast is permitted to “give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak and cause all who refused to worship it to be killed.”

The enforcement reaches the marketplace: “the second beast required all people, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead,” “so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark,” the name of the beast or the number of its name. And then the book does the thing its readers have never stopped doing: it invites the calculation. “Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666.” Candidates have been proposed in every century since, from emperors to institutions, and none has commanded the church's agreement. The telling leaves the number where the book leaves it: stated, calculated by its first hearers in their own world of numbered names, and unsealed by no one since.

title: Zion, Angels, and Harvests
subtitle: Revelation 14:1–20
description: The Lamb on Mount Zion with the marked-by-his-name 144,000; three angels with gospel, fall, and warning; a blessing for the dying; and two harvests of the earth.
paragraphs: Against the mark of the beast, the vision sets a forehead with different writing. “Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father’s name written on their foreheads.” Around them sounds a roar of waters and thunder that resolves into harps, and “they sang a new song before the throne” that belongs to them alone: “no one could learn the song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.” The book describes them in its own terms: undefiled, for they are virgins, and “They follow the Lamb wherever He goes. They have been redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb. And no lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless.”

Then three angels cross the sky with three announcements, the book's last evangel and its last warning side by side. The first carries “the eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on the earth,” to every nation and tribe and tongue and people, and its content is summons, not comfort: “Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come. Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters.” The second pronounces a fall before the story has shown it falling: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the passion of her immorality.”

The third is the severest speech in the book, and the telling does not dilute it: “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark on his forehead or on his hand, he too will drink the wine of God’s anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His wrath,” tormented in fire and sulfur before the holy angels and the Lamb, and “the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever. Day and night there is no rest for those who worship the beast and its image.” Set between the warning and what follows, the book addresses its own again: “Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.”

And immediately, a blessing for the dying: a voice orders John to write, “Blessed are the dead,” “those who die in the Lord from this moment on,” and the Spirit answers the beatitude aloud: “they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them.”

The chapter closes with two harvests swung like answers to each other. First the grain: “seated on the cloud was One like the Son of Man, with a golden crown on His head and a sharp sickle in His hand,” and an angel cries, “Swing Your sickle and reap, because the time has come to harvest, for the crop of the earth is ripe.” The earth is harvested. Then the grapes: another angel with a sharp sickle is ordered to “gather the clusters of grapes from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe,” and the vintage goes not to a cellar but to judgment: “he threw them into the great winepress of God’s wrath.” The winepress is trodden outside the city, “and the blood that flowed from it rose as high as the bridles of the horses for a distance of 1,600 stadia,” a river of blood some two hundred miles long, the book's most staggering image left to stand at its own scale.

title: The Song and the Bowls
subtitle: Revelation 15:1–16:11
description: The conquerors sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb; the temple fills with smoke; and the first bowls of wrath fall in the temple's own sequence.
paragraphs: The last series of judgments is introduced as the end of something: “seven angels with the seven final plagues, with which the wrath of God is completed.” Before the plagues move, the vision shows their far shore. John sees “something like a sea of glass mixed with fire,” and beside it stand the people the beast could not finish: “those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. They were holding harps from God.”

Their song carries two names, “the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb,” the Exodus sung again at a greater sea: “Great and wonderful are Your works, O Lord God Almighty! Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy. All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed.”

Then heaven's temple opens, “the tabernacle of the Testimony,” and the seven angels come out in clean bright linen with golden sashes, and the bowls are handed to them: “one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever. And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power; and no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” No intercession enters until the bowls are empty; the sanctuary itself is closed for the duration.

A loud voice from the temple gives the order: “Go, pour out on the earth the seven bowls of God’s wrath.” The first bowl targets the mark: “loathsome, malignant sores broke out on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” The second empties into the sea, “and it turned to blood like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died,” the trumpet's third become the bowl's whole.

At the third bowl, poured into rivers and springs until they too are blood, the book lets heaven defend the sentence in open court. The angel of the waters speaks first: “Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was, because You have brought these judgments. For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve.” And the altar itself answers, the altar under which the martyrs cried how long: “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.”

The fourth bowl is poured on the sun, “and it was given power to scorch the people with fire.” The response of the scorched is the trumpet chapters' refrain hardened: “they cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues. Yet they did not repent and give Him glory.” The fifth bowl goes onto the beast's own throne, “and its kingdom was plunged into darkness, and men began to gnaw their tongues in anguish” and curse the God of heaven, and the sentence lands a second time in the same words: “they did not repent of their deeds.” The bowls are more total than the trumpets, and the hearts under them, in the book's telling, are no softer.

title: Armageddon and It Is Done
subtitle: Revelation 16:12–21
description: The Euphrates dries, the kings assemble at Armageddon under a thief-in-the-night blessing, the seventh bowl declares it is done, and the great hail falls.
paragraphs: The sixth bowl dries a river into a road: “the sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” What comes down the road is gathered by deception, not force. “And I saw three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. These are demonic spirits that perform signs and go out to all the kings of the earth, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.”

In the middle of the gathering, the speaker interrupts his own vision with a blessing aimed at the reader, the book's sixth: “Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.” Then the assembly is named with the name that has echoed ever since: “they assembled the kings in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.” The chapter does not narrate the battle. The kings are gathered, the place is named, and the vision moves on; whatever Armageddon is in this book, its war is not described here, and the telling refuses to describe it for the book.

The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice comes from the throne in the temple with the shortest verdict in Scripture: It is done. What follows is the largest convulsion yet: “a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth,” so mighty that “The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed.” Babylon, promised her cup since the angels first named her fall, receives it now: “God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath.” Geography itself is undone: “every island fled, and no mountain could be found.”

Last falls the hail: “great hailstones weighing almost a hundred pounds each rained down on them from above.” And the response of the people under it is the refrain the book has been repeating since the trumpets, unchanged at the very end of the wrath: “men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.” The bowls are finished. The hearts, as the book tells it, are not.

title: The Woman on the Scarlet Beast
subtitle: Revelation 17:1–18
description: The great prostitute on the scarlet beast is explained by an angel: the beast in three tenses, the waters as peoples, and the woman as the great city.
paragraphs: Now the book pauses the action to explain a figure, and an angel issues the invitation: “Come, I will show you the punishment of the great prostitute, who sits on many waters. The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and those who dwell on the earth were intoxicated with the wine of her immorality.”

John is carried away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and what he sees is splendor arranged as an accusation: “a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was covered with blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was dressed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls,” holding “a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.” On her forehead a name is written, and the book calls it a mystery: “BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.” Beneath the finery, one fact darkens everything: “the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus.” John says he was utterly amazed, and the angel begins the explanation by questioning the amazement: “I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and ten horns.”

The beast's biography is a riddle in three tenses: “it was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the Abyss and go to its destruction.” Its career ends where the Abyss leads, and its reappearance will be a spectacle for the unlisted: “those who dwell on the earth whose names were not written in the Book of Life from the foundation of the world will marvel when they see the beast.”

Then the angel interprets the anatomy, and the telling follows his interpretations because they are the book's own: “This calls for a mind with wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. There are also seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come.” The beast itself is “an eighth king, who belongs to the other seven and is going into destruction.” The horns are “ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but will receive one hour of authority as kings along with the beast,” and “These kings have one purpose: to yield their power and authority to the beast.” Their campaign has one sentence of future written over it: “They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings,” and “He will be accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones.”

Two more of the angel's own glosses close the chapter. “The waters you saw, where the prostitute was seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues.” And the alliance will eat itself: “the ten horns and the beast that you saw will hate the prostitute. They will leave her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her with fire,” and the reason given is the darkest sovereignty statement in the book: “God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.” The angel's last identification is the one the telling rests on: “the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.” Readers have named her Rome in John's day, and other capitals and systems since; the angel's own description is what the vision hands us, and it is enough to carry into the fall that follows.

title: Fallen Is Babylon
subtitle: Revelation 18:1–24
description: Fallen, fallen is Babylon: the call to come out, the kings', merchants', and sailors' laments over her cargo, and a millstone hurled into the sea.
paragraphs: An angel descends with such glory that the earth is lit by it, and his cry is the second angel's announcement from the harvest chapter, now expanded into an obituary: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast.” The charges are read out: “All the nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her immorality. The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury.”

Before the sentence falls, a second voice speaks the book's tenderest command to its own people inside the doomed city: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues. For her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.” The sentence itself is measure for measure: “Give back to her as she has done to others; pay her back double for what she has done.” And her own voice is quoted as evidence against her, the boast standing as its own sentence: “I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.” Therefore, the voice says, “her plagues will come in one day,” death and grief and famine, “and she will be consumed by fire, for mighty is the Lord God who judges her.”

Then the chapter does something remarkable: it lets her mourners preach her funeral, three groups in turn, each standing at a distance for fear of her torment. The kings go first: “Woe, woe to the great city, the mighty city of Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”

The merchants' lament is an inventory, the longest cargo list in the Bible: gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls; fine linen, purple, silk, and scarlet; citron wood, ivory, bronze, iron, and marble; cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, and frankincense; wine, oil, flour, and wheat; cattle, sheep, horses, and carriages, and at the end of the manifest, priced like the rest, “of bodies and souls of slaves.” Their cry is for their market, not their friend: “The fruit of your soul’s desire has departed from you; all your luxury and splendor have vanished, never to be seen again.” “Woe, woe to the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls! For in a single hour such fabulous wealth has been destroyed!”

The sailors, every shipmaster and passenger and all who make their living from the sea, end the laments with a question no one answers: “What city was ever like this great city?” “Woe, woe to the great city, where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been destroyed.” Against all three woes, heaven is given the opposite instruction: “Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.”

A mighty angel seals it with an acted parable, hurling a stone the size of a great millstone into the sea: “With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again.” Then the silences are catalogued like the cargo was: “the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will never ring out in you again,” no craftsman, no millstone, no lamp, “and the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again.” The cause is named once more, and then the blood: “all the nations were deceived by your sorcery,” and “there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.”

title: Hallelujah and the White Horse
subtitle: Revelation 19:1–21
description: Heaven's hallelujahs, the marriage of the Lamb, the rider called Faithful and True on a white horse, and the swift capture of the beast and the false prophet.
paragraphs: Babylon's fall is answered in heaven with the book's only cluster of hallelujahs. A multitude roars the first: “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God! For His judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality. He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand.” The second answers it: “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.” The elders and creatures fall down with an Amen, a voice from the throne calls every servant small and great to praise, and the multitude sounds like waters and thunder for the fourth: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.”

The reign is celebrated as a wedding. “Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory. For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready.” Her clothing is interpreted by the book itself, as the bowls and waters were before: “the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints.” Then the angel gives John the seventh command to write a blessing, this one for the guest list: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” “These are the true words of God.”

John falls at the angel's feet, and is corrected the first of two times: “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus. Worship God!” The reason given has become a definition carried through church history: “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”

Then heaven opens for the rider. “I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war.” The description echoes Patmos and adds an army and a secret: “He has eyes like blazing fire, and many royal crowns on His head. He has a name written on Him that only He Himself knows. He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God.” Heaven's armies follow him in white linen on white horses, and “from His mouth proceeds a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and He will rule them with an iron scepter. He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.” On his robe and thigh one name is public: “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.”

The battle the kings were gathered for at Armageddon is introduced by the most terrible invitation in the book, an angel standing in the sun calling the birds to a rival feast: “Come, gather together for the great supper of God, so that you may eat the flesh of kings and commanders and mighty men, of horses and riders, of everyone slave and free, small and great.”

And then the war itself takes two verses: “the beast was captured along with the false prophet, who on its behalf had performed signs deceiving those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. Both the beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur.” “And the rest were killed with the sword that proceeded from the mouth of the One seated on the horse,” and the birds gorged themselves on their flesh. Nineteen chapters of gathering war end in capture, not combat; the book's climactic battle is won by arrest, and the telling lets the brevity stand as the statement it is.

title: The Thousand Years
subtitle: Revelation 20:1–6
description: The dragon is bound a thousand years; thrones and the souls of the beheaded reign with Christ; and the first resurrection is blessed, in the chapter's own sequence.
paragraphs: The dragon who started the war behind the war receives the beast's sentence in reverse order: arrest before judgment. “I saw an angel coming down from heaven with the key to the Abyss, holding in his hand a great chain. He seized the dragon, that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.” The disposal is thorough: “he threw him into the Abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him, so that he could not deceive the nations until the thousand years were complete.” And the limit is stated in the same breath as the binding: “After that, he must be released for a brief period of time.”

Then thrones, and souls. “I saw the thrones, and those seated on them had been given authority to judge,” and with them “the souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or hands.” The martyrs under the altar, the conquerors by the sea of glass, the refusers of the mark: the book gathers its witnesses into one scene. “And they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.”

The book then glosses its own event, carefully, the way it glossed the stars and the waters: “The rest of the dead did not come back to life until the thousand years were complete. This is the first resurrection.” And over the raised it pronounces one of the book's blessings: “Blessed and holy are those who share in the first resurrection! The second death has no power over them, but they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with Him for a thousand years.”

No chapter of the Bible has been mapped more differently than this one. Readers have taken the thousand years as a future reign of Christ on earth before the end, as the present age of the church's life in the world, and as a reign completed before Christ's return, and each reading has been held by serious Christians for centuries. The telling states what the chapter states, in the chapter's own order: a binding measured at a thousand years, mentioned six times in eleven verses, a first resurrection named by the book itself, and a release that must still come. The systems built on it belong to their builders; the scene belongs to John.

title: The Great White Throne
subtitle: Revelation 20:7–15
description: Satan's release, the last and shortest campaign, fire from heaven, the great white throne, the opened books and the book of life, and the second death.
paragraphs: The release announced in the binding arrives on schedule. “When the thousand years are complete, Satan will be released from his prison,” and his last work is the first work he ever did in the book, deceiving: he goes out “to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth,” Gog and Magog, the names the older prophet Ezekiel gave the final invader, “to assemble them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore.”

The last campaign is the shortest. “And they marched across the broad expanse of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. But fire came down from heaven and consumed them.” No battle is described; the encirclement is answered by fire, as the war of the white horse ended in arrest. And the deceiver's disposal is final this time: “the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, into which the beast and the false prophet had already been thrown. There they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.” The dragon, the beast, and the false prophet, the book's three engines of deception, are all in the lake, and the Abyss and the prisons are done with.

Then the last sight of the old order: “I saw a great white throne and the One seated on it. Earth and heaven fled from His presence, and no place was found for them.” Before the throne stand the dead themselves: “the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And books were opened, and one of them was the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books.”

Every hiding place for the dead is emptied into the court: “The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead, and each one was judged according to his deeds.” Then the jailers follow the prisoners into the sentence: “Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire.” The book names the sentence with its own gloss, split by its own dash and left here as it stands there: “This is the second death,” “the lake of fire.” And the last entry in the register is read out flatly: “if anyone was found whose name was not written in the Book of Life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.” The books of deeds and the Book of Life stand side by side to the end, and the vision of judgment closes without commentary. What comes next is not a verdict. It is a world.

title: I Make All Things New
subtitle: Revelation 21:1–8
description: A new heaven and a new earth; God's dwelling place with man; every tear wiped away; I make all things new; and the book's last severity spoken in the same voice.
paragraphs: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.” The sea, which in this book gave up monsters and armies and dead men, is simply absent from the new creation, its chaos retired with the old order. Into the new world comes the old vision's destination: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.”

The announcement that follows is the book's thesis spoken aloud, a loud voice from the throne: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.” The tabernacle language of the whole Bible, God pitching his tent among his people, is here made permanent and universal.

Inside that announcement sit the words the book is most loved for, and the telling gives them to the voice exactly as the voice gives them: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,” “and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.” The elder said it beside the throne in chapter 7 as a promise to the multitude; here the throne says it as the constitution of the new world.

Then the seated one speaks in his own person, the only time in the book he does so at length: “Behold, I make all things new.” And the writing command follows, grounded in the speaker's reliability: “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.” The book's beginning is echoed in its ending: “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.” And the overcomers of the seven letters receive their inheritance in the letter's own family language: “The one who overcomes will inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he will be My son.”

The same paragraph contains the book's last severity, and it stands at full strength next to the promises, as the outline of this whole telling requires: “But to the cowardly and unbelieving and abominable and murderers and sexually immoral and sorcerers and idolaters and all liars, their place will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. This is the second death.” The invitation and the exclusion are spoken by the same voice, in the same breath, to the same reader. The book will not have one without the other.

title: The Bride, the Wife of the Lamb
subtitle: Revelation 21:9–22:5
description: The bride shown from a high mountain: twelve gates and twelve foundations, the city measured with a golden rod, its defining absences, and the river of life.
paragraphs: One of the bowl angels returns with a different errand. The angel who carried John to see the prostitute on the beast now says the matching sentence: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” And the contrast is built into the geography: carried to a wilderness to see Babylon, “he carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high, and showed me the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, shining with the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, as clear as crystal.”

The city is described as measurement and memory together. “The city had a great and high wall with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and twelve angels at the gates,” three gates to each of the four directions. “The wall of the city had twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.” Israel's tribes on the gates, the Lamb's apostles in the foundations: the city is built out of the whole people of God, both covenants in one architecture.

The angel measures with a golden rod, and the dimensions are a cube magnified to a country: “The city lies foursquare, with its width the same as its length,” and “he measured the city with the rod, and all its dimensions were equal,” “12,000 stadia in length and width and height,” a cube some fourteen hundred miles on a side, the holy of holies rebuilt at the scale of the world. “And he measured its wall to be 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using.” The wall was jasper, the city pure gold like glass, and the foundations were adorned in order: jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, emerald, sardonyx, carnelian, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, chrysoprase, jacinth, and amethyst. “And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, with each gate consisting of a single pearl. The main street of the city was pure gold, as clear as glass.”

The absences define it as much as the measurements. “But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp.” The nations the beast once deceived now walk by that light, “and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory,” the same kings who warred and mourned, bringing their splendor in instead. “Its gates will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there.” And the gate rule is the last legal sentence of the old conflict: “nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life.”

Inside, Eden runs through the city like a river: “the angel showed me a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the main street of the city. On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” The tree Adam was barred from stands open on both banks, and its leaves treat the nations the dragon spent the book deceiving. “No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city, and His servants will worship Him. They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads. There will be no more night in the city,” and “the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.”

title: Yes, I Am Coming Soon
subtitle: Revelation 22:6–21
description: The book certifies its words, refuses to be sealed, warns at full strength, and ends in the exchange it traveled toward: yes, I am coming soon; amen, come, Lord Jesus.
paragraphs: The book closes by certifying itself and then refusing, pointedly, to be sealed. The angel's credential comes first: “These words are faithful and true. The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent His angel to show His servants what must soon take place.” And the speaker of the first letter's promise speaks the seventh and last blessing of the book: “Behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book.” Seven blessings stand across the book, from the reader and hearer of the first chapter to the robe-washers of the last, and keeping the words is how several of them are earned.

John, for the second time, falls at the angel's feet, and the correction is repeated word for word like a lesson he is meant to carry out of the vision: “I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who had shown me these things,” and the angel answers, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!”

Against Daniel, who was told to seal his book until the time of the end, John is told the opposite: “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near.” And the open book is left open among its hearers with the strangest pastoral saying in it: “Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous, and the vile continue to be vile; let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and the holy continue to be holy.” The nearness of the end does not coerce anyone in the book's last chapter; it reveals what everyone already is.

The coming is announced once more, with its justice attached: “Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.” And the last beatitude answers Laodicea's counsel to buy white garments: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates.” Outside the gates stands the final exclusion, in the same flat tone as the first: “outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.”

Then Jesus signs the book in his own voice, the only signature of its kind in Scripture: “I, Jesus, have sent My angel to give you this testimony for the churches. I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star.” And the book ends not with a warning but with an invitation thrown open to anyone thirsty: “The Spirit and the bride say, ’Come!’ Let the one who hears say, ’Come!’” and “let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.”

The warning stands guard over the whole invitation: “If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book,” and “if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book.” This telling has tried to stand under that warning rather than around it, moving the book's passages and never its words.

Last comes the exchange the whole book was traveling toward, promise and answer in two voices: “He who testifies to these things says, ’Yes, I am coming soon.’ Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” And over everyone who has read and heard, the final sentence is not a threat or a timetable but the greeting of the letters, grace: “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen.”
